title: Compound Inequalities (AND / OR)
subject: Algebra
objectives: Distinguish compound inequalities joined by AND from those joined by OR
Solve and graph AND (between) compound inequalities
Solve and graph OR compound inequalities
Translate real-world range and either/or conditions into compound inequalities

sections.heading: Two Conditions at Once
sections.content:
Lots of real situations involve two limits instead of one. A comfortable room temperature might be between 68 and 72 degrees — warmer than 68 AND cooler than 72, both at the same time. A carnival ride might require you to be taller than 48 inches AND shorter than 78 inches. These 'between' situations need two inequalities working together, and we call the result a compound inequality.

There are two ways to join inequalities, and they mean very different things. An AND compound inequality is satisfied only when BOTH conditions are true at once. 'Between 68 and 72' means a temperature has to clear both bars — above 68 and below 72 — so the solution is the overlap, the values that satisfy both. We often write an AND inequality in a compact three-part form, like 68 < t < 72, which literally reads 't is between 68 and 72.'

An OR compound inequality is satisfied when AT LEAST ONE condition is true. Think of a refund policy: you get a refund if an item is defective OR if you return it within 30 days — either one qualifies you. In math, 'x < -2 OR x > 5' is satisfied by any number that's either less than -2 or greater than 5; it doesn't have to be both. The solution is everything covered by either piece.

The key to this whole lesson is keeping AND and OR straight. AND means both must hold, so you look for the overlap (where the conditions agree). OR means either can hold, so you combine everything (where at least one condition is met). Get that distinction solid, and compound inequalities become very manageable, because solving each piece uses the exact inequality skills you already have.

rows: The OVERLAP of the two pieces — a segment between two points
AT LEAST ONE condition is true
The UNION of the two pieces — two rays often pointing apart
x is between two values, e.g. 2 < x ≤ 6
Two separate shaded rays going opposite directions

sections.heading: Solving AND Inequalities (the 'Between' Type)
sections.content:
An AND inequality often appears in three-part form, like -3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7. This single line is really two inequalities sharing a middle: -3 < 2x + 1 AND 2x + 1 ≤ 7. The variable expression is trapped in the middle, and we want to isolate the variable there.

The efficient way to solve the three-part form is to do the same operation to ALL THREE parts at once, keeping the variable in the middle. Whatever you do to the middle to peel away the constants and coefficient, you also do to the left part and the right part. It's the balance principle extended to three pieces instead of two: as long as you treat all three identically, the chain stays true.

For example, to solve -3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7, you'd first subtract 1 from all three parts, then divide all three by 2. The result is a clean 'between' statement telling you the range of x. The solution graphs as a single shaded segment connecting the two boundary points, because x must satisfy both ends simultaneously — it lives in the overlap.

One caution carries over from the last lesson: if you ever multiply or divide all three parts by a negative, you flip BOTH inequality signs in the chain. The flip rule still applies; it just applies to both symbols at once. Most of the time, though, AND inequalities are straightforward — operate on all three parts and read off the range.

sections.heading: How to Solve a Compound Inequality

steps.title: Decide whether it is AND or OR
steps.content: Read the problem to see if both conditions must hold (AND) or just one (OR). 'Between,' a three-part form, and 'and' signal AND; the word 'or' and conditions pointing to opposite extremes signal OR. This decision determines how you combine the solutions.

steps.title: For AND, operate on all three parts at once
steps.content: If the inequality is in three-part form like -3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7, isolate the middle by doing the same operation to all three parts. Keep the variable in the middle, and if you multiply or divide all parts by a negative, flip both signs.

steps.title: For OR, solve each inequality separately
steps.content: If the inequality is an OR, split it into its two inequalities and solve each one on its own using normal inequality rules. Then state the answer as 'first solution OR second solution.'

steps.title: Graph the overlap (AND) or the union (OR)
steps.content: Graph an AND solution as the overlap — usually a bounded segment between two points. Graph an OR solution as the union — usually two rays, often with a gap between them. Use open circles for < and >, filled circles for ≤ and ≥.

sections.heading: Solving a Three-Part AND Inequality
sections.content:
Solve -3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7.

Step 1 — Subtract 1 from all three parts to start isolating the middle:
  -3 - 1 < 2x + 1 - 1 ≤ 7 - 1
  -4 < 2x ≤ 6

Step 2 — Divide all three parts by 2 (positive, so no flip):
  -4 / 2 < 2x / 2 ≤ 6 / 2
  -2 < x ≤ 3

The solution is -2 < x ≤ 3, which reads 'x is greater than -2 and less than or equal to 3.' Graph: an open circle at -2 (because of <), a filled circle at 3 (because of ≤), and shading on the segment connecting them.

Check a value inside the range, like x = 0: 2(0) + 1 = 1, and -3 < 1 ≤ 7 is true. Check a value outside, like x = 5: 2(5) + 1 = 11, and 11 is not ≤ 7, so 5 is correctly excluded. The answer is a bounded segment because x has to satisfy both ends at once — that overlapping segment is the signature of an AND inequality.

sections.question: Solve the compound inequality 4 ≤ x + 2 < 9.
options: 2 ≤ x < 7, by subtracting 2 from all three parts
6 ≤ x < 11, by adding 2 to all parts
2 ≤ x < 9, by subtracting from only the left
sections.explanation: Subtract 2 from all three parts: 4 - 2 ≤ x < 9 - 2, giving 2 ≤ x < 7. You must apply the operation to all three parts, not just one, and this is an AND (between) inequality, not an OR.

sections.heading: Solving OR Inequalities
sections.content:
An OR compound inequality is written as two separate inequalities connected by the word OR, like 'x - 1 < -3 OR 2x > 10.' Because OR only requires one of the two conditions to be true, you solve each inequality on its own and then combine their solutions into one set.

So the method is simple: split the problem into its two inequalities, solve each one separately using your normal inequality skills, and then describe the full solution as 'this OR that.' You don't try to keep them in a single three-part line — OR inequalities can't be written that way, because their solutions often point in opposite directions and don't overlap.

The graph of an OR inequality is the union (the combining) of the two pieces — you shade everything that satisfies either one. Frequently this looks like two separate rays heading away from each other, with a gap in the middle. That gap is the region where NEITHER condition is true, so those values aren't part of the solution. For instance, 'x < -2 OR x > 5' shades far left and far right, leaving the middle (between -2 and 5) unshaded.

The contrast with AND is worth holding onto. AND gives you the overlap (often a segment in the middle); OR gives you the union (often two pieces spreading outward). Same individual solving steps — the difference is entirely in how you combine the results: overlap for AND, everything-covered for OR.

sections.heading: Solving an OR Inequality
sections.content:
Solve x - 1 < -3 OR 2x > 10.

Solve each piece separately.

First inequality:  x - 1 < -3
  Add 1 to both sides:
  x < -2

Second inequality:  2x > 10
  Divide both sides by 2:
  x > 5

Combine with OR: the solution is x < -2 OR x > 5. A number qualifies if it's either less than -2 or greater than 5 (it only needs to satisfy one piece).

Graph: an open circle at -2 with shading to the left, AND an open circle at 5 with shading to the right — two rays pointing in opposite directions, with the region between -2 and 5 left unshaded.

Check: x = -10 satisfies the first piece (-10 < -2), so it's in. x = 8 satisfies the second piece (8 > 5), so it's in. But x = 0 satisfies neither (0 is not < -2 and not > 5), so it's correctly excluded — it falls in the unshaded gap. This split-shading-with-a-gap is the classic look of an OR inequality.

sections.heading: AND Is the Overlap; OR Is the Union
sections.content: The biggest compound-inequality mistake is mixing up AND and OR graphs. AND means BOTH conditions hold, so the answer is the OVERLAP — usually a bounded segment between two points. OR means EITHER condition holds, so the answer is the UNION — usually two pieces, often with a gap between them. If you graph an AND as two spreading rays, or an OR as a single segment, the answer is wrong. Decide AND vs OR first, then graph the overlap or the union accordingly.

sections.heading: Let the Words Tell You AND or OR
sections.content: Watch the wording. 'Between,' 'at least ___ and at most ___,' and a value caught in the middle all signal AND (look for the overlap). 'Either,' 'at least ___ or no more than ___,' and conditions pointing to opposite extremes signal OR (combine both pieces). When a problem says a value must be in a single range, it's AND; when two separate situations each qualify, it's OR.

sections.heading: A Real-World Compound Inequality
sections.content:
A ride requires riders to be at least 48 inches but no more than 78 inches tall. Write and graph the heights that are allowed.

This is a 'between' situation — a rider must clear the lower limit AND stay under the upper limit — so it's an AND inequality. 'At least 48' means height h ≥ 48 (48 is allowed, so ≤/≥ with a filled circle). 'No more than 78' means h ≤ 78 (78 is allowed, filled circle). Combining both conditions in three-part form:
  48 ≤ h ≤ 78

Graph: a filled circle at 48, a filled circle at 78, and shading on the segment between them. The allowed heights are every value from 48 to 78 inches, including both endpoints.

Check: a 60-inch rider satisfies 48 ≤ 60 ≤ 78 — allowed. A 40-inch rider fails the lower limit (40 is not ≥ 48) — not allowed. An 80-inch rider fails the upper limit — not allowed. The single shaded segment captures exactly the riders who meet both requirements, which is what 'between two limits' always produces. Notice both endpoints are filled because the words 'at least' and 'no more than' include the boundary values themselves.

sections.question: Which compound inequality describes 'all numbers less than 1 or greater than 6,' and what does its graph look like?
options: x < 1 OR x > 6, two rays pointing outward with a gap between 1 and 6
x > 1 AND x < 6, the overlap between them
x < 1 AND x > 6, an empty solution
sections.explanation: 'Less than 1 or greater than 6' is an OR inequality, x < 1 OR x > 6, whose graph is two rays pointing in opposite directions with an unshaded gap between 1 and 6. Writing it as a single 'between' segment would describe an AND inequality, which is the opposite meaning.

sections.heading: AND = Both/Overlap; OR = Either/Union
sections.content: An AND compound inequality is true only when BOTH parts are true, so its solution is the overlap, often written in three-part form (like 2 < x ≤ 6) and graphed as a bounded segment. An OR compound inequality is true when AT LEAST ONE part is true, so its solution is the union, written as two separate inequalities and graphed as two rays. Solve each piece with normal inequality rules; the AND/OR only changes how you combine the results.

A compound inequality joins two conditions: AND requires both (its solution is the overlap, often a 'between' segment), while OR requires at least one (its solution is the union, often two rays) — and each piece is solved with ordinary inequality rules.

sections.heading: Ranges and Either/Or Conditions Are Everywhere
sections.content:
Compound inequalities show up the moment a real situation involves a range or a choice between conditions — which is constantly. Learning to express these precisely is a quietly powerful skill.

AND inequalities describe acceptable ranges, and ranges are how the world sets standards. A medication must be stored between 36 and 46 degrees. A healthy heart rate during exercise falls between target minimum and maximum values. A part manufactured for a machine must measure within a tolerance — at least the minimum size and at most the maximum — or it won't fit. A bridge is engineered to handle loads within a safe band. Body temperature, blood pressure, water pH for a pool, the speed limit range on a highway: all are AND inequalities, all 'between two limits.' When you write 36 ≤ t ≤ 46, you've captured an entire safety standard in one line.

OR inequalities describe situations where separate conditions each qualify. You get a scholarship if your GPA is above a cutoff OR your test score is above another. A thermostat turns on the heat if it's too cold OR the AC if it's too hot. An alert fires if a value drops too low OR climbs too high — exactly the logic in medical monitors, factory sensors, and weather warnings. The 'either extreme triggers a response' pattern is an OR inequality, and it's the backbone of how alarms and eligibility rules are built.

There's also a bridge to computer science here. The words AND and OR aren't just math vocabulary — they're the fundamental building blocks of logic that every computer program runs on. Every time an app checks 'is the user old enough AND did they agree to the terms?' or 'is the password too short OR does it lack a number?', it's evaluating compound conditions, the same AND/OR thinking you're practicing now. Master compound inequalities, and you've taken a real step toward the logical reasoning that powers both mathematics and the technology around you.

The biggest student error is graphing AND/OR backwards, so stress deciding AND vs OR first. For three-part AND inequalities, reinforce operating on all three parts simultaneously and flipping BOTH signs if dividing by a negative. Note the link to logical AND/OR in computer science.
